title: Springy Banks Pow Wow Grounds
summary: Springy Banks at Three Mile Harbor became an intertribal gathering place for powwows in 1944 and 1945, with later gatherings continuing into the early 1950s. Montaukett, Shinnecock, Matinecock, Narragansett, Schaghticoke, Cherokee, and other Native participants met there.
address_label: Springy Banks / Three Mile Harbor, East Hampton (general)
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: The Springy Banks gatherings show Native people building regional relationships during the mid-twentieth century, when public histories often spoke of Long Island's Indigenous communities only in the past. The powwows affirmed community, diplomacy, and continuing Native presence.
history_content:
Powwows were held at Springy Banks in 1944 and 1945 under the Long Island Council of the Federated Indian League. Ashby West, who used the name Red Thunder Cloud, was among the organizers. Montaukett, Shinnecock, Matinecock, Narragansett, Schaghticoke, Cherokee, and other Native people took part.

One gathering included a ceremonial "Treaty of Peace" signed by Narragansett leader Philip H. Peckham, known as Chief Night Hawk, and Montaukett leader Charles Butler, known as Chief Buckskin. Late-summer gatherings continued at Three Mile Harbor into the early 1950s and formed part of the regional powwow history in which Shinnecock participants also took part.

1

Montaukett family gatherings

Springy Banks, on Three Mile Harbor in East Hampton, was a place where Montaukett families from Freetown and Eastville gathered by the water. Olive Pharoah recalled these family reunions in a May 1996 conversation cited by historian John A. Strong. A photograph dated approximately 1935 shows members of the Butler and Pharoah families together. These gatherings expressed continuing family and community relationships; Native life here was not limited to public performances or ceremonial dress.

John A. Strong, The Montaukett Indians of Eastern Long Island (Syracuse University Press, 2001), p. 155; family photograph and identifications preserved in the Springy Banks collection.

Powwow ceremony and public visibility

The East Hampton Star’s August 31, 1944 report, “Peace Treaty Signing Feature of Indian Pow Wow,” described a public ceremony bringing Native participants together at Springy Banks. The ceremonial signing connected Montaukett and Narragansett people in the public account; it should not be read as a land sale or a surrender of Native rights. Alongside the performances and ceremony, the family photographs show named people maintaining community ties during a period when outsiders often represented the Montaukett as a people of the past.

East Hampton Star, August 31, 1944, “Peace Treaty Signing Feature of Indian Pow Wow”; article reproduced in the Hampton Waters Property Owners Association Winter 2022 newsletter.
